newsitem.title: USA: Dow soars after May jobs report soothes rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Dow soars after May jobs report soothes rate fears.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average soared into record territory Friday as Wall Street decided that the government's May employment report did not give the Federal Reserve enough reason to raise interest rates.

At 1:25 p.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 106.02 points, or 1.45 percent, at 7,411.31, after rising as high as 7,427.19 earlier. The blue-chip index's record close was 7,383.41 set on May 27.
In the broader market, advancing issues outpaced declines by a 15-7 margin on volume of 261 million shares on the NYSE. The Nasdaq composite index rose 7.09 points to 1,397.14.
Stock rose along with bonds. The 30-year Treasury rose 7/8 of a point, lowering its yield to 6.81 percent from 6.88 percent at Thursday's close. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"The market has decided the unemployment number could have been much worse," said Pierre Ellis, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics. "If the employment report had been strong across the board, the Fed would have appeared likely to tighten. Now it is confusing."

The Labour Department said 138,000 new jobs were created in May, lower than economists had expected and down from a revised 323,000 in April. The unemployment rate fell to 4.8 percent in May from 4.9 percent in April.
Market watchers said the data pointed to both an economic slowdown and a tighter labour market, which could make any interest rate increase harder to justify.

"The market needed to see slower employment growth, and it lucked out," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds. "This heightens the political pressure on the Federal Reserve not to raise rates."
The stock market was also gleeful because it believed the closely watched jobs report was its last major hurdle before the Federal Reserve's July meeting, analysts said.
"Numbers coming before the July meeting, like retail sales and inflation, don't look too powerful," Ellis said. "Some usual things which could go wrong don't look like they will."
Nearly all sectors took part in the rally, with interest-rate-sensitive financial and bank stocks surging, along with some high-technology shares, smaller stocks and energy and transport issues.
Short-covering contributed to stock market gains, said Dick Stein, vice president of U.S. Clearing Corp.
"This is as close as we've come in a while to a buying panic," he said. "A lot of people were licking their wounds."
But analysts remained cautious about the market's power.

"We would be careful up here," said Doug Cliggott, market strategist at J.P. Morgan. "The market has priced itself for the best of both worlds -- no change in interest rates with robust earnings. We might see one of these, but not both."

Bank stocks were particularly heartened by the bond market's stance, which pointed to lower long-term interest rates. They were also supported after brokerage PaineWebber Inc. initiated coverage of many banks with a buy rating.
Bank of New York Co. Inc. rose one to 44-1/8. NationsBank Corp. gained 2-1/8 to 63-7/8. Chase Manhattan added 2-3/4 to 100-1,/4 while BankBoston was up 1-7/8 at 75-1/4.

Shares of Excel Communications Inc. rose 1-1/2 to 20-3/8 after the company said it had a definitive agreement to acquire Telco Communications Group Inc. for about $1.2 billion. Telco's stock was up 4-3/4 at 26-3/4.
The New York Stock Exchange's limits on programme trading were activated when the Dow industrials rose more than 50 points.
The American Stock Exchange index added 2.42 points to 613.17.
